description_full: Karoon Energy Ltd operates as an oil and gas exploration and production company in Brazil, the United States, and Australia. The company holds 100% interest in the Santos Basin located in the Sáo Paulo, Brazil. Karoon Energy Ltd was formerly known as Karoon Gas Australia Ltd and changed its name to Karoon Energy Ltd in December 2018. The company was incorporated in 2003 and is based in Southbank, Australia.

financial_summary: KAROON ENERGY LTD. is a small-cap energy business with a $718M market cap on $629M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +18% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are contracting by -8.9pp, the first warning that competitive pressure is eroding the franchise.
Returns on capital run at 26% against a 9% cost of capital — a 17-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 55% confirm genuine pricing power.
The company is burning through $37M of cash, and without positive owner earnings any valuation rests on hope rather than evidence.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.8× net debt/EBITDA, and thin 2.2× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 11.2% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.5× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 27% operating margin runs 11pp above the Energy median (16%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.47x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.05 across 203 companies in the universe; the top four hold 40% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 7% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 7% over the last three months.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 36% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 57% and a beta of 0.70, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.30 vs 5y 0.37), so read it loosely.
Trading is thin (about $1K a day), below the $1.0M liquidity floor flagged; building a position would move the price.
In past sell-offs it fell 80% in the 2020 crash and 42% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades 34% below its DCF fair value of $1.56, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 26%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $1.07 to $2.29 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Energy peers: P/E 9.4 vs 13.6 and EV/EBITDA 3.0 vs 7.1 (sector median).
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of -5.2% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 17.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The price implies 21.5% annual cash-flow growth, 7pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 26% clears the cost of capital of 9.1% by 17pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.51).
It runs a 55% gross margin and burns cash (FCF margin -6%).
ROE of 12% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.7x equity multiplier).
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.8x net debt to EBITDA ($206.1M of cash against $338.8M of debt), and interest cover is thin at 2.2x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.11 in the distress zone.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 17.7% over 3 years.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.9%, and institutions hold 65%.
It returns 11.2% a year to shareholders (6.3% in buybacks and 2.9% in dividends).
people: With about 167 employees, each generates about $3.8M of revenue, 1.9x the Energy median.
Free cash flow is negative, at -$222K per employee.
CEO pay is $909K (0x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
